title: Age-predicted maximal heart rate revisited
authors: Tanaka H, Monahan KD, Seals DR
journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
population: Healthy adults: meta-analysis of group means from 351 studies (492 groups), plus laboratory cross-validation in 514 healthy subjects
findings: Meta-analysis of 351 studies, 492 groups and 18,712 subjects: HRmax strongly related to age (r = -0.90), regression HRmax = 208 - 0.7 x age.
Laboratory cross-validation in 514 healthy subjects gave 209 - 0.7 x age, virtually identical to the meta-analytic equation.
The regression line was not different between men and women, nor influenced by wide variation in habitual physical activity.
The authors state the then-current 220 - age equation underestimates HRmax in older adults.
Meta-analysis: HRmax strongly related to age (r = -0.90), equation HRmax = 208 - 0.7 x age.
Laboratory study (n=514) gave 209 - 0.7 x age, virtually identical to the meta-analysis.
The regression line did not differ between men and women and was not influenced by wide variations in habitual physical activity.
limitations: Meta-analysis of group means, so the equation says nothing about individual spread (the abstract gives no SD or SEE). Healthy, mostly non-athletic adults; not runner-specific.
implications: Use 208 - 0.7 x age as the default HRmax prior when no measured or observed maximum exists; do not use 220 - age.
No sex or training-status adjustment of the HRmax estimate is justified by this paper.

Treat the estimate as a population mean with wide individual error (see Nes 2013 for SEE and Shookster 2020 for poor individual agreement) and replace it with an observed maximum as soon as data exist.
If no measured maximum is available, seed HRmax with 208 - 0.7 x age rather than 220 - age, treated as a prior with about +/-10 bpm uncertainty.
Replace the prior with the highest reliably recorded wearable heart rate from hard efforts once enough data exist (guard against optical sensor artefacts).
Do not adjust HRmax for sex or habitual activity level.
